title: Mathy (or Sciency or Historyish) Moments (Valued Within Exercise)
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart profiles a Valued Within exercise borrowed from teacher Adam Craig: a weekly homework assignment in which students hunt for a "mathy moment" -- a real-world example connecting to class content -- and report back on Mondays. He describes his own adaptation, "History in Real Life," in his world history classes, and shares several actual student responses connecting family 9/11 memories, the history of volleyball, and constitutional language in political ads to their coursework. He argues the assignment's power lies in its low-stakes, high-frequency structure: it's perceived as easy homework, but it consistently trains students to notice and articulate connections between class content and everyday life. The piece closes by noting how widely teachers across content areas have adapted the core idea once introduced to it.
points: The core structure -- a standing weekly assignment to spot a subject-relevant "moment" in daily life -- creates its own peer accountability, as Stuart notes students eventually chide classmates who can't find one.
Stuart's own adaptation ("History in Real Life") shows the technique transferring cleanly from math to a humanities subject, evidence for its cross-curricular flexibility.
The student response excerpts demonstrate the assignment working as intended: unprompted personal reflection (a parent's 9/11 memory, volleyball's history) rather than rote fact recall.

He frames the exercise's value as compounding because of its low perceived cost to students -- "an easy homework assignment" that nonetheless habituates them to notice course-relevant meaning in everyday life.
quotes: Each weekend, Adam's students have a simple homework assignment: find a mathy moment in real life. On Monday, Adam asks his students to report out what they found.

Within a month or so of doing this, students in class will roll their eyes when one of their peers says, "I couldn't find a mathy moment." They'll chide the IDKer, saying things like: "C'mon, didn't you have to be anywhere on time?
An example of World History in my life was when I asked my mom and dad a couple days ago of where they were during 9/11. My mom told me that she was at work and my dad said that he was sleeping.

Every single day I am going to volleyball practice and it makes me wonder how volleyball came to be. I think all the time of how volleyball has evolved and how it's become such an important thing in my life.
The cool thing with Adam's idea is that, once students get used to it, it's perceived as an easy homework assignment, and it gets them looking for and thinking about your subject in everyday life.
